meta.date_display: the Twenty-Fifth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

news.subhead: THE PACIFIC DESK, EMPTIED: THE EASTERN SHELF SELLS ITS TWO GRANDEST LOTS IN A SINGLE DAY — SATO CARRIES HIS TRIPLE CROWN TO WRIGLEY FOR SIX YEARS AND ONE HUNDRED TWENTY MILLIONS, TAIRA TAKES HIS IMPOSSIBLE FASTBALL TO TORONTO FOR FIVE YEARS AND FOURSCORE, AND THE FIRST OF DECEMBER COLLECTS ITS ACCOUNTS EARLY
news.body:
The first of December has stood over the eastern market all week like a bailiff at the door, and on Tuesday the house sold its two grandest lots rather than test him. The slugger Teruaki Sato, the finest bat the posting season carried, agreed with the Cubs on a contract of six years and $120 million, by the account of sources — pending a physical, the club not confirming.[^bastian-sato] Within hours the right-hander Kaima Taira, whose unlikely fastball these columns put under the instruments only yesterday, agreed with the Blue Jays on five years and $80 million, an opt-out standing after the third season, likewise unannounced.[^matheson-taira] The reader will recall the clock beneath both courtships, set down in yesterday's Pacific column: should the labor agreement die on the first of December with no successor, the posting windows die with it — and the date has concentrated minds, as the prospect of hanging is said to do.

The man Chicago bought is 27, swings left-handed, and arrives wearing the Central League's Triple Crown: a .306 average, 39 home runs and 106 runs driven in for the Hanshin Tigers this past season, with 40 doubles, a .383 on-base figure and a .609 slugging mark besides. He is a five-time All-Star of the Japanese game, twice the Central League's Most Valuable Player, and took a Gold Glove at third base in 2025; the strikeouts that once shadowed the profile thinned a shade this past year, the rate easing to 26.7 percent while the walks climbed to 11.1. Third base in Chicago belongs to Alex Bregman for four seasons yet, so the newcomer projects to a corner of the outfield and the designated hitter's post — which is to say, into the twin vacancies left by Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ, both at liberty. The wire reaches naturally for the Murakami comparison — the last man before Sato to wear an NPB Triple Crown, likewise a left-handed power bat, who struck 35 home runs as a rookie sensation for the White Sox — while noting the differences in kind: Sato the more aggressive swinger, with rather more contact in the zone; Murakami the more selective, with more walks and more missing.[^bastian-sato]

The purchase wants two annotations from the Herald's own files. First, the arithmetic: between Monday night and Tuesday the Cubs committed $240 million — five years and $120 million to the left-hander Trevor Rogers, as yesterday's columns recorded, and now six and $120 million to Sato — answering inside a single day both the emptied rotation and the emptied outfield these columns have inventoried all week. Second, the standing of the handicappers: industry sources had the Sato field narrowed only yesterday to the Yankees, the Phillies and the Jays, the Cubs expressly shorn from it — and the Cubs signed him all the same, though the wire's other prophecy, The Athletic's word that the signature would land before Thanksgiving, is hereby proven with room to spare. The club's long Japanese groundwork — the Suzuki purchase of 2022, Imanaga's after it, the scouting network the president Jed Hoyer has tended for years — did not wait upon the odds-makers' permission.[^bastian-sato][^rumors24]

Toronto's purchase is the bolder wager and the neater fit. Taira is likewise 27, stands 5-foot-8, and comes from the Seibu Lions, for whom he pitched this past season to a 1.36 earned-run average across 146 innings — the best figure in all Nippon Professional Baseball — with a fastball that touches 99 and departs, as yesterday's anatomy had it, from a slot only Joe Ryan undercuts among regular big-league starters, released further down the mound than most men a half-foot taller manage. The Toronto desk reaches for Marcus Stroman, the 5-foot-7 Jay of 2014 through 2019, then withdraws the comparison as quickly: Stroman lived on the ground ball, where Taira's trade is the swing and the miss. The rotation now reads Cease, Taira, Yesavage and Soriano, with Ponce fifth and Miles behind — respectable company for a club that finished 79-83 and last in its division — and the shopping is understood to turn next to the batting, where the need is absolute, no club in the majors having scored fewer runs. Suzuki remains the obvious fit, which would dress three Japanese stars in Toronto flannels beside Okamoto; and the Herald notes the wider arc, for this is the establishment whose losing Skubal bid of $420 million came to light only yesterday, now spending its consolation deliberately.[^matheson-taira] What remains of the eastern shelf is chiefly one man: the Sawamura laureate Hiromi Itoh, lately seen calling in Chicago, his window shorter than ever.[^rumors24]

news.subhead: THE INK DESK: BALTIMORE LOSES ONE ACE AT MIDNIGHT AND ANNOUNCES HIS SUCCESSOR BY SUPPER — PERALTA, LAUREATE OF OCTOBER, TAKES ONE HUNDRED TWENTY-FIVE MILLIONS OVER FIVE YEARS, THE RICHEST PITCHING PAPER IN THE BIRDS' LONG LEDGER
news.body:
The Orioles lost Trevor Rogers to the Cubs late Monday night; they had his successor signed and announced before Tuesday was out. The club made official a five-year contract with the right-hander Freddy Peralta — $125 million by a source's account, carrying a $10 million signing bonus and wages of $23 million a year — and the sum is the largest Baltimore has ever committed to a pitcher, third on the franchise's all-time bill behind only Chris Davis's seven years and $161 million of 2016 and Pete Alonso's five and $155 million of last December. The president of baseball operations Mike Elias called the man "a winning player who understands what it takes to compete and succeed on the biggest stage," and thanked the control owner David Rubenstein for the resources — not idly, for five of the eight largest contracts in the club's history have been signed since August of 2025, the checkbook having opened with the new ownership.[^rill-peralta]

The signature closes a courtship these columns began counting on Sunday, when The Athletic numbered seven clubs in pursuit — the Rays seriously engaged on the man they restored, with the White Sox, the Cubs, the Friars and the Jays besides, and two establishments that kept their names to themselves — and the reader will observe that Baltimore's name never appeared in print at all; whether the Birds were one of the two anonymous bidders or a late arrival, the wire does not say, and either way the mystery resolves in orange. What they bought is October's laureate: "Fastball Freddy," 30 years old, twice an All-Star, nine seasons in the majors and the most of them in Milwaukee, whose 2026 ran the whole dramatic register — a 4.99 figure across 22 starts in Queens, a deadline passage to Tampa Bay, a 3.25 across ten starts down the stretch, and then the Most Valuable Player's honors of the league championship series on one earned run in 12 innings against the Lake Erie men, the heater that averages 94.3 miles an hour in summer sitting 97 and touching 99 in the autumn chill. October was not spotless — the Brewers reached him for five runs in Game 3 of the World's Series — but by then the laurels were banked.[^rill-peralta]

He joins a rotation got up largely of men who once held his new distinction: Kyle Bradish's five years and $90 million of July and Shane Baz's five and $68 million of March were each, briefly, the richest pitching paper in Birdland, and both now pitch behind the record's newest holder, with the right-hander Brandon Young likely in company and the fifth post contested between the left-hander Povich and the prospect Gibson. The club, a spectator to the last two postseasons, is understood to want one more starter yet, ideally left-handed; the formal introduction comes Monday at Camden Yards.[^rill-peralta]

news.subhead: THE LABOR QUESTION: SIX MORNINGS REMAIN — THE LEAGUE WITHDRAWS ITS ESCROW CLAUSE AND PRONOUNCES EVERY GUARANTEED DOLLAR SAFE, THE UNION'S AUDIT FINDS THE SAME DOLLAR MERELY COLLECTED A YEAR LATER, AND THE CAP BENEATH THE GILT STANDS WHERE IT STOOD
news.body:
The bargainers' Tuesday produced a concession from the league and an unimpressed ledger from the union, which has become the week's established ratio. Major League Baseball withdrew the escrow provision from its salary-cap proposal — the mechanism, borrowed from the other leagues, by which a slice of every wage is held back against the season's final accounting — and declared that under its cap-and-floor design every guaranteed contract, new or existing, remains guaranteed in full, with no player money withheld at all. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal," said the spokesman Glen Caplin, "removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the new Salary Cap and Floor system" — the union having argued for months that escrow was the end of the guaranteed contract by another name.[^feinsand-escrow]

The union read the fine print aloud. Under the amended design, any aggregate overpayment to the players in one season is folded into the computation of the cap and floor in the seasons following, and after an overpayment the league may reckon those figures against revenues lagged as much as two years — which is, the interim executive director Bruce Meyer observed, not holding the money back this year but taking the same sum from players' pockets the next. "It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap — to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement," he said, calling the offer one more proposal that "pits player against player, past, present, and future." The Herald's ledger-keeping on this question is of long standing and unchanged: the frame beneath every gilding remains a fixed pot, and the agreement that governs the game has 6 mornings left to live, expiring at one minute before midnight on the first of December. The week's furious signing calendar, set down above and below, is the market's own commentary on that date.[^feinsand-escrow]

news.subhead: THE EXCHANGE DESK: WHAT REMAINS ON THE SHELVES — KING IS TIPPED TO SIGN INSIDE THE WEEK, SIX CLUBS BID FOR LOWE'S FIVE-AND-THIRTY HOME RUNS, THE CAPITAL NINE JOIN THE CHISHOLM QUEUE, AND NEITHER CHICAGO NOR QUEENS CALLS ITS SHOPPING FINISHED
news.body:
With Rogers, Peralta and Taira all off the board inside a day's span, Michael King stands this morning as the best starting pitcher at liberty, and the wire does not expect him to stand long: the insider Jon Paul Morosi said Tuesday he believes "wholeheartedly" that King finds a home by the end of this week. The queue is familiar — the Cubs and the Mets both linked, the Friars reported eager to bring their old right-hander home, and the Jays interested, though whether the Taira purchase retires that pursuit the wire cannot say. Behind him the position market stirs. Brandon Lowe, late of Pittsburgh and his 35 home runs, has six clubs in some measure of pursuit by Morosi's count — the Yankees, the Birds, the Jays, the Rays, the Friars and the Phillies — with a draft pick owed the Corsairs when he signs elsewhere, the qualifying offer having been declined; and Jazz Chisholm Jr., who spoke with eleven clubs at the GM Meetings, adds the Nationals to a queue already holding the Jays and the Mets, the wire weighing a down year with the bat — a 97 OPS+ — against a plus glove, 41 stolen bases, and a 30-30 season two years back.[^rumors24]

The two spending clubs, for their part, decline to be finished. In Chicago, ESPN's Jesse Rogers reckons the Cubs "probably sign one more starter" and then mind their bullpen once the agreement expires — Clay Holmes and David Peterson, who each finished the season in Cubs flannels, both in play — while the door on a Shota Imanaga reunion is reckoned shut after conversations earlier this winter. And in Queens the Mets, their rotation crowned and their first base minded, still shop for arms — judiciously, The Athletic reports, the club discussing two-year terms with pitchers who ask three, with Mahle, Boyd and Imanaga among the earlier conversations and King among the present interests — and have shown at least some level of interest in Chisholm besides, though the second-base post nominally belongs to Marcus Semien for two years more.[^rumors24]

news.subhead: THE MOTOR CITY DESK: GLOVES FOR THE ARMS — KIM, A GOLD GLOVE MAN LATELY UNDONE BY ICE AND INFIRMARY, TAKES ONE YEAR AND FIVE MILLIONS TO TIGHTEN THE DETROIT INFIELD, AND MELTON'S SIX-YEAR FORTUNE IS SIGNED WITH THE SAND OF A SPOILED MAUI HOLIDAY STILL IN HIS SHOES
news.body:
The Tigers' president of baseball operations Scott Harris hinted Tuesday morning that a move for the infield defense was in the works; the ink wanted barely two hours to appear. Detroit agreed with the veteran shortstop Ha-Seong Kim on one year and $5 million, with another $1 million in incentives, pending a physical and unconfirmed by the club. The file is a study in what injury does to a resume: Kim at his peak, with the 2022 and 2023 Padres, was worth 5.0 and then 5.4 wins above replacement and took a Gold Glove; what followed was a shoulder operation that swallowed the better part of a year, and then this past season's absurdist misfortune — a right middle finger lacerated in a slip upon the ice in his native South Korea, operated upon in the spring, inflamed again in July — and a .116 average over 51 games for Atlanta when upright. The Tigers buy the glove and the bounce-back at the bottom of the market: Kim takes shortstop in rotation with Kevin McGonigle, the league's reigning Rookie of the Year,[^bref-awards] whose defensive figures argue for more of his time at third base in any case.[^beck-kim]

The same morning, at Comerica Park, the club made official the six-year, $46.5 million extension of the right-hander Troy Melton, recorded in Saturday's edition of these columns, and the ceremony supplied the anecdote the terms deserved: Melton was in Maui with his girlfriend when the talks turned serious, and conducted a fortune's negotiation from a holiday. "I kind of ruined a Maui vacation a little bit, ruined a sunset cruise and a dinner, but I think it was worth it," the man allowed. "So maybe we'll go back to Maui someday and not be on the phone so much." The instrument is the longest Detroit has given a pitcher since Verlander's seven-year extension commencing in 2013, and it climbs as the man is expected to: wages of $1 million in each of the first two years, rising by steps to $18 million in 2032, with a club option for 2033 at $23 million and escalators that could carry the late years higher. Melton, who turns 26 on the third of December, pitched to a 2.76 earned-run average this past season — a run of 14 starts at 1.49 after his May return from elbow inflammation among it — and Harris pronounced the thesis of the whole Detroit desk in two sentences: "We're going to continue to add arms. We also want to protect these arms."[^beck-melton][^beck-kim]

news.subhead: THE INK DESK, SMALLER TYPE: A CATCHER KEEPS HIS ONLY FLANNELS IN THE QUEEN CITY, CLEVELAND PAYS SEVENTEEN MILLIONS AND A HALF FOR ONE YEAR OF A MENDED LEFT ARM, TAYLOR CROSSES CHICAGO TO BALANCE THE PALE HOSE OUTFIELD, AND SANTANA, RISING ONE-AND-FORTY, SAILS BACK TO THE SOUND
news.body:
The day's smaller signatures covered the map. In Cincinnati, Tyler Stephenson — seven seasons a Red, the club's first selection in the 2015 draft, and one of the few catchers of any standing on the open market — agreed to stay for three years and $30 million, an opt-out standing after the second year, pending a physical. The season that earned it was his sturdiest: a career-best 2.5 wins above replacement, 15 home runs, a bat the adjusted figures rate a hair above the league's common run, and blocking work the instruments rank in the 97th percentile — though the same instruments mark the rest of the glovework at nine runs below par, so the purchase is the bat, the blocks and the incumbency.[^stepansky-stephenson] In Cleveland, the Guardians paid a premium for a single year of Kris Bubic, $17.5 million, betting that the arm which made an All-Star of him in 2025 — a 2.55 earned-run average in 20 starts for Kansas City, rebuilt around a changeup hitters batted .119 against this past season — outlasts a 2026 spent four months on the shelf with elbow and shoulder complaints. He joins a company fronted by Gavin Williams, whose 248 strikeouts led the league, and the young Parker Messick, runner-up in the Rookie of the Year balloting and third in the Cy Young voting,[^bref-awards] on the only staff in the majors that ran four starters to 30 starts apiece.[^stebbins-bubic]

In Chicago, Tyrone Taylor changed sides of town without changing cities: two years and $17 million from the White Sox, whose outfield — left-handed and switch-hitting nearly to a man, Brenton Doyle excepted — wanted precisely a right-handed bat of his description. Taylor, 32, remade his swing this past season and hit .279 with a .502 slugging mark and a 128 OPS+ between the Mets and the Cubs, batting .351 after the deadline carried him to Wrigley and posting a .921 on-base-plus-slugging against left-handed pitching; he brings besides a plus glove at all three outfield posts, an arm the instruments place in the 85th percentile, and a sprint the years have not yet taxed.[^greenspan-taylor]

And in Seattle, sentiment signed a minor-league contract. Carlos Santana, who turns 41 in April, returns to the Mariners with an invitation to spring camp — his third tour in the organization, counting the ten days of December 2018 when he was traded in and flipped out again — to stand as insurance behind Josh Naylor at first base and as something less measurable in the clubhouse, where his 2022 vintage furnished the win-dance, the home-run helmet, and a three-run clout in Toronto that turned a Wild Card series. The bat is nearly spent — eight games and two hits for Arizona this past season — but the Puget Sound men are weighing what a presence of his standing offers a camp, and a minor-league promise costs nothing to find out.[^kramer-santana]

desk_note: A Wednesday paper of emptied shelves: the Pacific courtships these columns have carried since the posting bells of early November both closed in a single day, Baltimore crowned its costliest arm by nightfall, and the bargainers traded an escrow clause for a colder ledger — the whole of it set down above. The forward ledger was fetched before a word was written, as the house custom commands, and reads as it has all week: the camps' reporting dates remain unposted, so the count runs to the first rung bearing a date — the spring exhibition openers of Friday, the 19th of February, 86 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow on Wednesday, the 24th of March, 119 mornings off.[^bref] The nearer columns press: the collective agreement has 6 mornings left to live; the republic carves its Thanksgiving bird on the morrow, and the before-the-feast prophecy on Sato, carried in yesterday's columns, is proven above with room to spare; Cooperstown's committee of sixteen reports in 11; the Winter Meetings convene at San Diego with the Rule 5 drafting on December 9, 14 mornings from this one; and the writers' envelope waits for the 19th of January, 55 mornings off. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
